in 2000, for example, only 4.7 percent of all commuters utilised public tra
reason is that most such commuting is limited to a few large. densely settled regions with
extensive fixed-rail systems, something relatively rare in the US. In the unlikely event that
the USA's existing public transit capacity were tripled and fully utilized, morning private
vehicle trips would fall by only 8 percent — certainly a step forward, but hardly enough to
end congestion = and tripling public transit capacity would have enormous public spending
implications. There are many good reasons to expand the nation's public transit systems to
aid mobility, but doing so will not notably reduce either existing or future peak-hour traffic
congestion.
Many planners recommend constraints on urban growth. They suggest encouraging
population growth within existing neighborhoods which could then be more efficiently
served by public transit, although most residents of those neighborhoods vehemently oppose
this approach. But in any case, as most regions are already too underpopulated to support
much public transit, this strategy would unfortunately have a very limited impact.
The third approach to congestion would be to build sufficient road capacity to accommodate
all drivers wanting to travel in peak hours at the same time without delays. But this ‘cure’ is
both highly impractical and prohibitively expensive. Governments would have to widen all
major commuting roads by, in effect, turning most of every metropolitan region into giant
superhighways. Those would then be grossly underutilized during non-peak hours. There are
occasions when adding road capacity is sensible, but attempting to build enough to
completely eliminate peak-hour congestion is simply futile.
